editorial_contributions.text:
Quoted from the authors introduction: ``Let \(X\subset\mathbb{P}^n\) be a smooth projective variety over a number field \(F\). Fix a height function 
\[
H: \mathbb{P}^n(F)\to \mathbb{R}_{>0}
\]
 and consider the counting function 
\[
N(X,T)= \{x\in X(F)\mid H(x)\leq T\}
\]
 Manin's conjecture and its refinements predict asymptotic formulas for \(N(X^0,T)\), as \(T\to\infty\), where \(X^0\subset X\) is an appropriate Zariski open subset of an algebraic variety with sufficiently positive anticanonical class. Of particular importance are equivariant compactification of algebraic groups and their homogenous spaces.

 In all equivariance cases considered previously, it was essential that \(X\) admits an action, with a dense orbit, of a solvable algebraic group.

 In this paper, we establish these conjectures for a new class of varieties, which includes nonspherical varieties under a technical assumption on automorphic characters.''

 The explicit result is the following: ``Let \(H\) be a connected simple algebraic group defined over a number field \(F\), \(G=H^n\) its \(n\)-fold product. Let \(X\) be a smooth projective \(G\)-equivariant compactification of \(X^0:= H\setminus G\), where \(H\) acts on the left diagonally, with boundary \(X\setminus X^0\) a divisor with strict normal crossings. Under this technical assumption (on automorphic characters) \(X\) satisfies Manin's conjecture and its refinements.''

 (Note: The polarization which gives the rise to the embedding of \(X\) into \(\mathbb{P}^n\), is the anticanonical class \(-K_X\).)

title.title: Multiple mixing for adele groups and rational points

editorial_contributions.text:
A \(\mathbb{C}\)-valued function \(\phi\) on a group \(G\) is said to be of positive type if, for any choice of elements \(g_1, \cdots, g_n \in G\), the matrix \((\phi(g_i^{-1}g_j)) \in M_n(\mathbb{C})\) is positive semi-definite. Such a function \(\phi\) normalized to satisfy \(\phi(e)=1\) is called a trace on \(G\) if it is a class function. The set \(Tr(G)\) of traces is a compact, convex subset of the unit ball of \(\ell^{\infty}(G)\). Its extreme points constitute the set \(Char(G)\) of characters of \(G\). (It should be noted that in the literature what is called character is called trace in this paper).

 In this paper, the authors completely determine Char\((G)\) for \(G = \mathcal{G}(k)\) where \(\mathcal{G}\) is a connected algebraic group defined over a number field \(k\) and \(G\) is generated by its unipotent one-parameter subgroups. The case of semi-simple \(\mathcal{G}\) is easy and the authors consider a general \(G\) as above. In terms of a Levi decomposition of \(\mathcal{G} = LU\), there is a Levi decomposition \(G = (L \cap G(k))(U \cap G(k))\). The set Char\((G)\) is described in terms of some data attached to \(L\) and the action of \(L \cap G(k)\) on the Lie algebra of \(U\). The idea is to analyse the restriction of an element of Char\((G)\) to \(U\). An essential step consists of classifying \(G(k)\)-invariant ergodic probability measures on an adelic solenoid \(\mathbb{A}^d/\mathbb{Q}^d\) which is naturally associated to \(G(k)\). The authors use Ratner's measure rigidity results for homogeneous spaces of \(S\)-adic Lie groups. This appears to be the first instance of an application of Ratner's rigidity theorems in a set-up involving operator algebras.

title.title: Characters of algebraic groups over number fields

editorial_contributions.text:
The topological covering groups of locally compact groups, and in particular, the reductive or semi-simple groups over local and global fields, appear naturally in number theory. As one of the earliest examples, the modular forms of half-integral weight, such as the Jacobi theta function and other more general theta functions, correspond to automorphic forms on the covering groups of the special linear group.

However, the constructions of those groups, and their representation theory, harmonic analysis on them and the theory of automorphic forms, was not developed systematically so far. The problem is that from the point of view of the Langlands program, one should be able to construct correspondences between the representations of the covering groups and certain representations on the Galois side, as well as the local and global functorial liftings between different groups. The topological definition of the covering groups does not provide a good framework for such considerations.

The key insight comes from the theory of \textit{J.-L. Brylinski} and \textit{P. Deligne} [Publ. Math., Inst. Hautes Étud. Sci. 94, 5--85 (2001; Zbl 1093.20027)]. They construct a large class of topological covering groups, including all classically important examples, in an algebraic way, providing a promising framework for the development of the Langlands program for the covering groups. At the end of the first paper in this volume, the authors quote Deligne's hope expressed in the letter to the third author dated Dec. 14, 2007, which says:

``For me, the aim is to understand `metaplectic' forms on semi-simple groups, the hope being that they are not `new' object, but rather correspond to usual automorphic forms on some other groups, on which they give new information. I would like to have precise conjectures on the hoped for correspondence, and I view my paper with Brylinski as setting a landscape in which conjectures should fit.''

This Astérisque volume, inspired by Deligne's hope, takes precisely that task -- to develop the necessary formalism on the Galois side in the case of topological covering groups of the Brylinski-Deligne class, formulate the Langlands program for such covering groups, which is referred to as the Langlands-Weissman program, and provide evidence for the Langlands correspondence in that setting. The volume consists of four papers:
\begin{itemize}
\item W. T. Gan, F. Gao and M. H. Weissman, L-groups and the Langlands program for covering groups: a historical introduction, pp.~1--31.

\item M. H. Weissman, L-groups and parameters for covering groups, pp.~33--186.

\item W. T. Gan and F. Gao, The Langlands-Weissman program for Brylinski-Deligne extensions, pp.~187--275.

\item M. H. Weissman, A comparison of L-groups for covers of split reductive groups, pp.~277--286.
\end{itemize}
The first paper serves as an introduction to the subject, but also provides an excellent historical account of the construction of topological covering groups, the development and the state-of-the-art of their representation theory, harmonic analysis and the theory of automorphic forms. It also describes the setting of the Brylinski-Deligne theory, and explains the properties expected of the Langlands correspondence for covering groups.

This historical introduction begins by recalling a classic paper of \textit{C. C. Moore} [Publ. Math., Inst. Hautes Étud. Sci. 35, 5--70 (1968; Zbl 0159.03203)], in the construction and classification of the central extensions of a locally compact group by a locally compact abelian group. In particular, the question of the existence and the role of the universal central extension of a locally compact group and its fundamental group is emphasized. In the case of the abstract Chevalley groups, the seminal work of \textit{R. Steinberg} [Générateurs, rélations et revetements de groupes algébriques. Centre Belge Rech. math., Colloque Theor. Groupes algebr., Bruxelles 1962, 113--127 (1962; Zbl 0272.20036); Lectures on Chevalley groups. New Haven, CT: Yale University (1968; Zbl 1196.22001)] is recalled. The covering groups over a local field are considered in the case of split groups, [\textit{C. C. Moore}, Publ. Math., Inst. Hautes Étud. Sci. 35, 5--70 (1968; Zbl 0159.03203); \textit{H. Matsumoto}, Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Supér. (4) 2, 1--62 (1969; Zbl 0261.20025)], quasi-split groups [\textit{V. V. Deodhar}, Am. J. Math. 100, 303--386 (1978; Zbl 0392.20027)] and general \(k\)-isotropic groups [\textit{G. Prasad} and \textit{A. S. Rapinchuk}, Publ. Math., Inst. Hautes Étud. Sci. 84, 91--187 (1996; Zbl 0941.22019)] which is based on the previous work of Prasad and Raghunatan. In the case of adèlic groups, the main global theorem of Prasad and Rapinchuk [loc. cit.] is recalled.

The authors then proceed to introduce the Brylinski-Deligne class of covering groups. The main point of the Brylinski-Deligne construction of covering groups is to consider the central extensions of group sheaves, instead of topological groups. They introduce and classify the multiplicative \(\mathbb{K}_2\)-torsors over an algebraic group sheaf \(\mathbb{G}\) in the Zariski site of a scheme, i.e., the central extensions \[ 1\longrightarrow \mathbb{K}_2\longrightarrow \widetilde{\mathbb{G}}\longrightarrow \mathbb{G}\longrightarrow 1 \] of \(\mathbb{G}\) by the \(K\)-theory sheaf \(\mathbb{K}_2\) defined by Quillen. For a fixed \(\mathbb{G}\), the classification problem reduces to the classification of the Picard category of multiplicative \(\mathbb{K}_2\)-torsors over \(\mathbb{G}\). This is achieved in terms of three invariants, considering the enhanced root datum similar to the classification of split linear algebraic groups, which depends functorially on \(\mathbb{G}\).

Given a local field \(k\), taking \(k\)-points preserves the exactness of the above exact sequence, and then pushing it out by the norm residue symbol from \(\mathbb{K}_2(k)\) to the roots of unity \(\mu(k)\), gives rise to a topological central extension by \(\mu(k)\) \[ 1\longrightarrow \mu(k) \longrightarrow \widetilde{G}\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow 1 \] of a locally compact group \(G\) of \(k\)-points. Given a global field \(k\) with the ring of adèles \(\mathbb{A}\), in the same way one obtains a central extension \[ 1\longrightarrow \mu(k)\longrightarrow \widetilde{G}_{\mathbb{A}}\longrightarrow G_{\mathbb{A}}\longrightarrow 1 \] of the adèlic group \(G_{\mathbb{A}}\) by \(\mu(k)\), which comes with a canonical splitting in \(G_{\mathbb{A}}\) of the group \(G_k\) of \(k\)-points, so that the automorphic forms can be defined in this setting.

This ends the discussion regarding the constructions of topological covering groups, and the authors turn to the overview of the results present in the literature. They recall the work of \textit{A. Weil} [Acta Math. 111, 143--211 (1964; Zbl 0203.03305)] on the Segal-Shale-Weil representation, \textit{T. Kubota} [J. Math. Soc. Math. 148, No. 6, 1655--1694 (2012; Zbl 1325.11046)] over a \(p\)-adic field, the work of several people, including Bump, Friedberg, Hoffstein and their students and collaborators, on the Fourier coefficients of metaplectic Eisenstein series and generalized theta functions, \textit{G. Savin} [Math. Ann. 280, No. 2, 185--190 (1988; Zbl 0644.22007); J. Reine Angew. Math. 566, 111--134 (2004; Zbl 1032.22006)] on the Iwahori Hecke algebra for covers of simply-connected groups, which gives the correspondence between genuine representations with Iwahori-fixed vectors of the cover and of certain linear group, \textit{J. Adams} and \textit{R. Herb} [Represent. Theory 14, 70--147 (2010; Zbl 1235.22020)] on the local character identities for coverings of real groups, the work of Harish-Chandra for real groups, which is not limited to linear groups, gives the classification of discrete series representations and the Plancherel theorem for covers of real Lie groups, \textit{W.-W. Li} [Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Supér. (4) 45, No. 5, 787--859 (2012; Zbl 1330.11037)] on the results of Harish-Chandra for covers of \(p\)-adic groups, \textit{C. Luo} [Math. Res. Lett. 24, No. 6, 1759--1774 (2017; Zbl 1412.22034)] on the theory of \(R\)-groups and the Howe's finiteness conjecture for invariant distributions for covering groups, \textit{D. Ban} and \textit{C. Jantzen} [Glas. Mat., III. Ser. 48, No. 2, 313--334 (2013; Zbl 1304.22019); Glas. Mat., III. Ser. 51, No. 1, 153--163 (2016; Zbl 1356.22016)] on the Langlands' quotient theorem and the Casselman criteria for square-integrability and temperedness for covering groups, \textit{C. Mœglin} and \textit{J.-L. Waldspurger} [Spectral decomposition and Eisenstein series. Cambridge: Cambridge Univ. Press (1995; Zbl 0846.11032)] on the theory of Eisenstein series on covering groups, and \textit{W.-W. Li} [Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Supér. (4) 45, No. 5, 787--859 (2012; Zbl 1330.11037); Can. J. Math. 64, No. 3, 497--537 (2012; Zbl 1273.11087); Math. Ann. 356, No. 3, 1029--1064 (2013; Zbl 1330.11038) J. Reine Angew. Math. 686, 37--109 (2014; Zbl 1295.22027)] on the Arthur-Selberg trace formula for covering groups.

The first paper in this volume ends with a discussion of the main ingredients of the classical Langlands program and the expectations of the Langlands program for the covering groups, which is referred to as the Langlands-Weissman program. These ingredients are the dual and the L-group and the theory of endoscopy. The generalization of these two notions to the Brylinki-Deligne covering groups would mean the beginning of the program. The construction of the L-group for Brylinski-Deligne covers, and providing evidence that the constructed L-group fits into the expected local Langlands correspondence for covering groups (LLCC), is the subject of the remaining papers in this volume.

The second paper in the volume consists of four parts. The aim of Part I is to define the dual group and the L-group of the Brylinski-Deligne coverings of a quasi-split reductive group over a local or global field \(F\). For a fixed positive integer \(n\), it is always assumed that the group \(\mu_n\) of \(n\)th roots of unity in \(F\) is of order \(n\). Given a Brylinski-Deligne central extension \(\widetilde{\mathbb{G}}\) of \(\mathbb{G}\) by \(\mathbb{K}_2\), the pair \(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}=(\widetilde{\mathbb{G}},n)\) is referred to as a degree \(n\) cover of \(\mathbb{G}\).

As mentioned above, there are three invariants classifying Brylinski--Deligne central extensions. The L-group \({}^{\mathrm{L}} \widetilde{G}\) of the cover \(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}\) is defined in terms of these three invariants, the integer \(n\), a fixed injective complex character \(\varepsilon\) of \(\mu_n\), which is the character defining \(\varepsilon\)-genuine representations, and a fixed separable closure \(\overline{F}\) of \(F\). It is an extension by the dual group \(\widetilde{G}^\vee\) of the Galois group \(\mathrm{Gal}_F\) of the field extension \(\overline{F}/F\). There is no canonical splitting of the L-group, although it often splits, which reflects the fact that there is no canonical \(\varepsilon\)-genuine representation such as the Steinberg or the trivial representation. The dual group \(\widetilde{G}^\vee\) is a pinned complex reductive group with the action of \(\mathrm{Gal}_F\) by pinned automorphisms, which was already considered in various forms [\textit{M. Finkelberg} and \textit{S. Lysenko}, J. Inst. Math. Jussieu 9, No. 4, 719--739 (2010; Zbl 1316.22019); \textit{P. J. McNamara}, Prog. Math. 300, 299--327 (2012; Zbl 1283.11081); \textit{R. C. Reich}, Represent. Theory 16, 345--449 (2012; Zbl 1302.22014); \textit{J. Adams} et al., J. Am. Math. Soc. 20, No. 3, 701--751 (2007; Zbl 1114.22009)]. In the center \(\widetilde{Z}^\vee\) of \(\widetilde{G}^\vee\), there is a \(2\)-torsion element \(\tau_Q(-1)\) required in the construction of the L-group.

The construction of the \(L\)-group \({}^{\mathrm{L}} \widetilde{G}\) begins with the metaGalois group \(\widetilde{\mathrm{Gal}}_F\), which is a two-fold extension of \(\mathrm{Gal}_F\) with the canonical cocycle defined by the quadratic Hilbert symbol, and proceeds with two twists. The first twist is obtained as the push out of the metaGalois group via the central 2-torsion element mentioned above, which gives the extension \[ 1\longrightarrow \widetilde{Z}^\vee \longrightarrow (\tau_Q)_\ast \widetilde{\mathrm{Gal}}_F \longrightarrow \mathrm{Gal}_F \longrightarrow 1. \] The second twist is obtained using the étale fundamental group of certain étale gerbe \(\mathbf{E}_\varepsilon(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}})\) as the extension \[ 1\longrightarrow \widetilde{Z}^\vee \longrightarrow \pi_1^{\mathrm{et}}(\mathbf{E}_\varepsilon(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}})) \longrightarrow \mathrm{Gal}_F \longrightarrow 1. \] The paper contains a useful appendix in which the necessary preliminaries regarding torsors and gerbes are recalled. The L-group is then defined as the extension \[ 1\longrightarrow \widetilde{G}^\vee \longrightarrow {}^{\mathrm{L}} \widetilde{G} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Gal}_F \longrightarrow 1. \] obtained as the push out to \(\widetilde{G}^\vee\) of the Baer sum of the two extensions of the Galois group \(\mathrm{Gal}_F\) by \(\widetilde{Z}^\vee\).

Once the L-group is defined, the author checks that it behaves well under passing to Levi subgroups, between local and global fields, and rings of integers in the non-archimedean case, and that it is functorial with respect to a certain class of homomorphisms referred to as ``well-aligned'' homomorphisms. The Weil and Weil-Deligne parameters over the local field \(F\), the unramified parameters over the ring of integers \(\mathcal{O}\) of \(F\) in the non-archimedean case, and the conjectural global parameters are introduced.

Part II of the second paper of the volume deals with the representation theory. Given the cover \(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}\) of Brylinski-Deligne class, and the character \(\varepsilon\), the irreducible admissible \(\varepsilon\)-genuine representations of the central extension over the local field \(F\), the \(\varepsilon\)-genuine automorphic representations of the central extension of the adèlic group, and the irreducible spherical representations of the central extension with respect to \(G^\circ=\mathbb{G}(\mathcal{O})\) are defined. The necessary results regarding the representation theory in this context are either recalled or adapted if necessary. Certain notions are slightly modified, such as the central core character.

The author proceeds to discuss the local Langlands conjecture for covering groups, abbreviated as LLCC. It should be a finite-to-one parametrization of the equivalence classes of irreducible admissible \(\varepsilon\)-genuine representations of the central extension \(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}\) over a local field \(F\) by the set of the \(\widetilde{G}^\vee\)-orbits of the Weil parameters in \({}^\mathrm{L} \widetilde{G}\) satisfying certain compatibility conditions, similar as in the classical local Langlands conjectures.

The LLCC is then tackled in several cases, which provides evidence that the L-group is well chosen, and that the LLCC satisfies some of the expected conditions. The first case is the case of so-called sharp covers of split tori over a local or global field and the ring of integers in the non-archimedean case. It occupies the whole Part III of the paper. In that case, the parametrization is a bijection, compatible with pullbacks of covers via isomorphisms and for Baer sums of covers. For the general case of the split tori, the parametrization may not be surjective.

The remaining cases form Part IV of the second paper. The second case is a parametrization of the spherical representations for the cover of a quasi-split group over \(\mathcal{O}\). It is bijective, and follows from the Satake isomorphism for covering groups, the result for the sharp covers of split tori, and tracking the Weyl group actions.

The third case is the case of a sharp double cover of an anisotropic torus over \(\mathbb{R}\). The parametrization is bijective in this case, and provides evidence regarding the correct choice for the gerbe in the definition of the L-group.

The fourth case is the case of a double cover of a semi-simple quasi-split group over \(\mathbb{R}\). In that case the finite-to-one parametrization of discrete series representations is obtained, based on the Harish-Chandra parametrization of discrete series, the parametrization for double covers of anisotropic tori, and tracking the involutions of the Weyl group.

At the end of the introduction to the second paper in the volume, a list of further open questions is provided, as well as certain useful philosophical principles underlying the Langlands program for covering groups.

The third paper in this volume considers the Brylinski-Deligne covering groups of a split reductive group over a local or global field \(F\). Let \(\widetilde{\mathbb{G}}\) be a Brylinksi-Deligne central extension of the split reductive algebraic group \(\mathbb{G}\) by \(\mathbb{K}_2\). In the case of a split group, the L-group can be defined in simpler terms than in the case of quasi-split groups of the second paper in the volume. In particular, it avoids the use of the notion of étale gerbes. This definition is also due to the third author of the volume, as the authors of this paper follow the ideas of his letter to Deligne dated June 2, 2012. It is still assumed that the group of \(n\)th roots of unity in the field \(F\) is of order \(n\).

The L-group of a Brylinski-Deligne covering of a split reductive group was previously defined by \textit{M. H. Weissman} [Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 368, No. 5, 3695--3725 (2016; Zbl 1369.14058)], based on the work of \textit{P. J. McNamara} [Prog. Math. 300, 299--327 (2012; Zbl 1283.11081)], in terms of Hopf algebras. This definition is more complicated than the one presented in this paper, and gives the correct L-group only for a subclass of Brylinski-Deligne covering groups. However, the general construction by M. H. Weissman of the L-group for quasi-split groups in the second paper of this volume gives in the split case the L-group isomorphic to the L-group constructed in this paper. This fact is the subject of the fourth paper in this volume, as elaborated below.

Let \(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}\) be the \(n\)-fold topological covering group arising from the Brylinski-Deligne central extension \(\widetilde{\mathbb{G}}\), as above. The L-group is then defined as an extension \[ 1\longrightarrow \widetilde{G}^\vee \longrightarrow {}^\mathrm{L}\widetilde{G}\longrightarrow W_F\longrightarrow 1 \] of the Weil group of \(F\) by the dual group \(\widetilde{G}^\vee\). The dual group is the same as in the second paper of this volume. The extension should be functorial and compatible with passage to Levi factors. As already mentioned, unlike the linear case, even if the extension splits, it has no canonical splitting.

The purpose of this paper is to discuss some properties of the L-groups for Brylinski-Deligne covers of split groups, introduce a slightly modified variant, provide further evidence for its correctness, and introduce the automorphic \(L\)-functions for covers. It shows that the L-group extension splits, but is not always isomorphic to a direct product of the dual group and the Weil group. The latter is illustrated by a simple example, which exhibits several interesting phenomena. For example, it also shows that the covering group of Brylinski-Deligne class is not always split over a hyperspecial maximal compact subgroup. Furthermore, the set of distinguished splittings of the L-group of the Brylinski-Deligne covering of a split group is defined. For a subclass of such covers, it is shown that the set of distinguished splittings exists, thus generalizing the results of \textit{M. H. Weissman} [Trans. Am. Math. Soc. 368, No. 5, 3695--3725 (2016; Zbl 1369.14058)] in the case \(n=2\) and \(n\) odd.

It is also proved that distinguished splittings of the L-group \({}^{\mathrm{L}}\widetilde{G}\) are in natural bijection with distinguished genuine characters of the center of the covering of a maximal \(F\)-split torus of \(G\). These characters are explicitly given in terms of the Weil index and the \(n\)th Hilbert symbol. They are used to define the principal series representations and generalize the work of \textit{G. Savin} [J. Reine Angew. Math. 566, 111-134 (2004; Zbl 1032.22006)].

The L-parameters for \(\widetilde{\mathbf{G}}\) are the \(\widetilde{G}^\vee\)-orbits of the splittings of the short exact sequence defining the L-group \({}^\mathrm{L} \widetilde{G}\). Using this notion of L-parameters, the LLCC is formulated. It is then verified in the case of covering tori, for unramified representations and metaplectic groups. Already in the simple example mentioned above, it seems natural to define the L-group of several closely related Brylinski-Deligne coverings, instead of dealing with each of them separately. Thus, the authors proceed by proposing a slightly modified definition of the L-group to handle this issue.

The next goal of the paper is to define the automorphic \(L\)-functions for a global Brylinski-Deligne covering group. As in the Langlands-Shahidi method, given a representation \(R\) of the L-group, one should define the automorphic \(L\)-function associated to \(R\). However, because there is no canonical splitting of the L-group in the case of covers, it is necessary to fix a distinguished splitting and define the relative L-parameters with respect to the fixed splitting. The automorphic \(L\)-functions associated to the representation \(R\) and the fixed splitting are then defined using these relative L-parameters. It is shown by \textit{F. Gao} [Am. J. Math. 140, No. 1, 83--137 (2018; Zbl 1425.11109)] that the Langlands-Shahidi type of automorphic \(L\)-functions appear in the constant term of the Eisenstein series on the Brylinski-Deligne covering groups, and have a meromorphic continuation.

The authors point out certain anomalies in the representation theory of the considered covering groups and explain how they can be explained in terms of the L-groups. The first anomaly is observed in the case of the metaplectic group, for which there exist representations in the same L-packet with a different central character. The second anomaly is that in the restriction of an irreducible genuine representation of the Kazhdan-Patterson cover of \(\mathrm{GL}_r\) to the cover of \(SL_r\), the irreducible summands are not always in the same L-packet.

Finally, the authors turn to the instances of the Langlands functoriality. They discuss the possible endoscopic groups of a Brylinski-Deligne covering group, and explain that the notion of isomorphism of endoscopic data should be modified. The notion of base change is carefully defined based on the work of \textit{E. A. Bender} [Proc. Am. Math. Soc. 40, 63--65 (1973; Zbl 0243.12008)] and the local base change constructed for covering tori.

The paper ends with a series of illustrative examples for the discussed notions, and a list of basic open questions, which are in authors' opinion crucial for further development of the Langlands-Weissman program.

The fourth paper in this volume compares the L-groups used in the second and the third paper. In the second paper, the L-group is defined in terms of gerbes for covers of quasi-split reductive groups over a local or global field. The L-group in the third paper is defined in simpler terms, based on an unpublished letter by the third author of this volume to Deligne, dated June 2, 2012, but only for covers of pinned split reductive groups over a local or global field. The purpose of this paper is to show that the two constructions yield isomorphic L-groups in the case of covers of split groups, so that the results in different papers of this volume are indeed compatible, and provide evidence for the same LLCC.

In conclusion, this excellently written Astérisque volume will certainly become the key reference in the theory of covering groups, and in particular, their representation theory, the theory of automorphic forms and the emerging Langlands-Weissman program. It will serve as the gateway into the subject for young mathematicians, and the starting point for all future developments. I strongly believe that this volume will speed-up the research in this area, and significantly contribute to the fulfillment of Deligne's expectations quoted above.

editorial_contributions.text: The paper is concerned with integral models of algebraic tori over algebraic number fields together with the comperison of properties of the models. It depends on the scheme which represent the (Néron, Voskresenskií) model under consideration. The author offers a setting for the Néron model of an algebraic torus, namely the standard or the canonical integral models of the torus. The basic result concerns the Néron model of a maximal algebraic torus unaffected in a semisimple algebraic group. Integral models of algebraic tori over Dedekind schemes are presented in the book by \textit{S. Bosch} et al. [Néron models. Berlin etc.: Springer-Verlag (1990; Zbl 0705.14001)], in papers by \textit{V. E. Voskresenskij} [Math. Notes 44, No. 3--4, 651--655 (1988; Zbl 0699.20037); translation from Mat. Zametki 44, No. 3, 309--318 (1988)], by \textit{S. Bosch} and \textit{Q. Liu} [Manuscr. Math. 98, No. 3, 275--293 (1999; Zbl 0934.14029)] and by \textit{S. Yu. Popov} [Vestn. Samar. Gos. Univ., Mat. Mekh. Fiz. Khim. Biol. 2001, No. 4(22), 85--108 (2001; Zbl 1072.14529)]. Let \(T\) be an algebraic torus over a field \(k\), \([L:k]\) its splitting field, \(G = {\mathcal Gal}(L:k)\). Section 1 introduces \(G\)-module \(\hat T\) of rational characters of \(T\), its coordinate ring \(k[T] = L[\hat T]^G\) and affine realization of \(T\). Section 2 concerns definitions of (Voskresenskií, canonical integral, standard integral) models of algebraic tori. Section 3 gives some indications on algorithms of constracting of Néron models of algebraic torus over global field of characteristic 0 and over its localizations. Section 4 presents properties of standard integral model over a number field and of the corresponding models over local fields. The last section contains interesting observations on a family of algebraic tori of a special structure and concludes with an explicit representation of the Néron model of a maximal algebraic torus unaffected in a semisimple algebraic group with the root system \(B_n\). It would be interesting to know how the author's work relates to \textit{A. Mézard}, \textit{M. Romagny} and \textit{D. Tossici} [Ann. Inst. Fourier 63, No. 3, 1055--1135 (2013; Zbl 1297.14051)] solution under the construction of models of \((\mathbb{G}_{m,K})^n\). (Mézard, Romagny, Tossici assume that \(K\) is the fractional field of a discrete valuation ring and note that ``we set up a precise, nontrivial dictionary that indicates how to translate the congruences in a discrete valuation ring of characteristic 0 on one side, into congruences in a discrete valuation ring of characteristic \(p\) on the other side''. They present models of \((\mathbb{G}_{m,K})^n\) constructed by successive extensions of affine, smooth, one-dimensional models of \(\mathbb{G}_{m,K}\) with connected fibers, called filtered group schemes).

editorial_contributions.text:
In a series of papers [J. Reine Angew. Math. 686, 37--109 (2014; Zbl 1295.22027); Ann. Sci. Éc. Norm. Supér. (4) 45, No. 5, 787--859 (2012; Zbl 1330.11037); Math. Ann. 356, No. 3, 1029--1064 (2013; Zbl 1330.11038); Ann. Inst. Fourier 64, No. 6, 2379--2448 (2014; Zbl 1315.11041)] the author has generalized the invariant Arthur-Selberg trace formula to an \(m\)-fold central extension \(\widetilde{G}\) of \(G(\mathbb{A})\), where \(G\) denotes a connected reductive algebraic group defined over a number field \(F\), and \(\mathbb{A}\) is the ring of adéles of \(F\). This formula presents an equality between two genuine invariant distributions, i.e., the geometric and spectral sides of the trace formula.

In the paper under the review, the author takes an important step further and stabilizes the Arthur-Selberg trace formula for \(\widetilde{G}\), thus extending the results established for connected reductive groups by \textit{J. Arthur} in [J. Inst. Math. Jussieu 1, No. 2, 175--277 (2002; Zbl 1040.11038); Invent. Math. 143, No. 1, 157--220 (2001; Zbl 0978.11025); Ann. Math. (2) 158, No. 3, 769--873 (2003; Zbl 1051.11027)].

We denote the endoscopic group by \(G^{!}\) and let \(\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ell}}(\widetilde{G})\) be the set of elliptic endoscopic data of \(\widetilde{G}\).

Let \(V_{\mathrm{ram}}\) denote the finite set consisting of all Archimedean places, the dyadic places, and certain non-Archimedean places. Let \(V\) stand for a finite set of places such that \(V_{\mathrm{ram}} \subset V\). Let \(I\) stand for an invariant genuine distribution on \(\widetilde{G}_V\) which intervenes in the invariant trace formula for \(\widetilde{G}\). The author then considers its stable counterparts \(S^{G^{!}}\) on \(G^! (F_V)\) for various \(\mathbf{G}^! \in \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ell}}(\widetilde{G})\), and defines the endoscopic counterpart of \(I\) as 
\[
I^{\mathcal{E}}(f) = \sum_{\mathbf{G}^! \in \mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{ell}}(\widetilde{G})} 2^{- \#(\mathrm{SO-factors~in~}G^! )} S^{G^!}(f^!).
\]
The test function \(f\) is here transferred to \(G^!\) taking \(\otimes\)-products, denoted by \(f \mapsto f^!\).

The authors proves that \(I_\nu = I^{\mathcal{E}}_\nu\) as genuine invariant distributions on \(\widetilde{G}_V\), for any infinitesimal character \(\nu\), and analogously for the spectral and discrete case. Thus, the invariant trace formula for metaplectic groups is decomposed into a linear combination of stable trace formulas of products of split odd orthogonal groups via endoscopic transfer. This provides the first fully stabilized trace formula in the Langlands-Weissman program involving a nontrivial theory of endoscopy.

The obtained stabilization is based on authors' earlier work, and presents an extension of the methods used by \textit{C. Moeglin} and \textit{J.-L. Waldspurger} in the linear case [Stabilisation de la formule des traces tordue. Vol. 1. Basel: Birkhäuser/Springer (2016; Zbl 1361.11004); Stabilisation de la formule des traces tordue. Vol. 2. Basel: Birkhäuser/Springer (2016; Zbl 1381.11001)], following the long inductive process which includes series reinterpretations needed in the metaplectic case.

After introductory part and preliminaries on the covering groups and their representation theory, the author review the formalism of endoscopy for the groups of metaplectic type, followed by some results on the Archimedean transfer and the combinatorial summation formula. Harish-Chandra descent of endoscopy, also known as semisimple descent, which presents one of the most important tools in this work, is studied in section 4, while section 5 is devoted to the stabilization of invariant weighted orbital integrals. A theory of germs in the metaplectic case is developed in section 6, where the stabilization of weighted Shalika germs and weighted fundamental lemma are also obtained. Sections 7 and 8 are devoted to weighted characters in non-Archimedean and Archimedean case, and the construction in the Archimedean case, which happens to be more complicated, continues in section 9. In section 10 the author switches to the global trace formula and expresses the global geometric coefficients in the particular form, whose matching is settled in section 11 using the global descent. In section 12 the invariant local trace formula is considered and its endoscopic counterpart is provided. The stabilization is reduced to the key geometric hypothesis, which is proved in section 13. Invariant weighted characters are introduced in section 13, followed by their stabilization and the global spectral stabilization. Also, section 13 contains proofs of all main theorems.

The breadth of the presentation also makes this paper a valuable reference for researchers in the field.
